title: I/O, Buses & Interrupts
summary: How the CPU talks to keyboards, disks, and network cards — over buses, and without wasting cycles waiting for them.

blocks.markdown:
The CPU spends most of its life talking to things slower than itself — disks, keyboards, network cards. **I/O (input/output)** is that traffic, and a **bus** (a shared set of wires) carries it.

- The core question: how does the CPU know a device is ready, without wasting cycles checking?
- Three answers: **polling**, **interrupts**, and **DMA**.
- Get this wrong and a fast CPU still feels slow.

blocks.subTitle: What a bus is
blocks.markdown:
A **bus** is a shared set of wires that lets the CPU, memory, and devices exchange signals. Only one message travels per wire group at a time, so devices take turns.

Every bus carries three kinds of signal:

- **Address bus** — which location or device to talk to.
- **Data bus** — the actual bytes being moved.
- **Control bus** — read/write, timing, and interrupt signals.

blocks.subTitle: System vs peripheral buses
blocks.markdown:
Not all buses are equal — they sit at different distances from the CPU.

| Bus | Connects | Speed |
|---|---|---|
| System bus | CPU, memory, cache | Fastest |
| Peripheral bus | Disks, USB, network cards | Slower |

A **bridge** chip moves signals between the two so slow devices don't hold up memory traffic.

blocks.subTitle: PCIe at a glance
blocks.markdown:
**PCIe (Peripheral Component Interconnect Express)** is the peripheral bus most modern machines use for GPUs, SSDs, and network cards.

- Unlike an old shared bus, each device gets its own **point-to-point lane** to a controller — no waiting for others to finish.
- More lanes per device means more bandwidth, which is why GPUs demand many lanes.

See [cpu-datapath](cpu-datapath) for how the CPU side connects in.

blocks.subTitle: Memory-mapped vs port-mapped I/O
blocks.markdown:
The CPU needs addresses to reach a device's registers. Two schemes exist.

| Scheme | How it works |
|---|---|
| Memory-mapped I/O | Device registers share the normal memory address space; use regular load/store |
| Port-mapped I/O | Devices get a separate address space; special IN/OUT instructions only |

Memory-mapped I/O is more common today — no special instructions needed.

blocks.subTitle: Programmed I/O (polling)
blocks.markdown:
**Programmed I/O** means the CPU itself moves every byte, checking a device's status register in a loop — called **polling** — until it's ready.

- Simple to build, no extra hardware.
- Wastes CPU cycles spinning on slow devices; a keyboard press might make it poll millions of times for nothing.

blocks.subTitle: Interrupt-driven I/O
blocks.markdown:
With **interrupt-driven I/O**, the CPU starts a device and moves on to other work. The device raises an **interrupt** — a signal on the control bus — only when it's actually ready.

- No wasted polling loops.
- Cost: each interrupt still pulls the CPU off its current work to handle it.

blocks.subTitle: DMA (direct memory access)
blocks.markdown:
**DMA (direct memory access)** is a separate controller that copies data straight between a device and memory — bypassing the CPU entirely for the transfer itself.

- The CPU just tells the DMA controller *source, destination, length* and returns to other work.
- The DMA controller raises one interrupt when the whole block is done, not per byte.
- Essential for disks and network cards moving large blocks.

The core trade-off in I/O design.

| | Polling | Interrupts |
|---|---|---|
| CPU cost when idle | Wastes cycles checking | Free — CPU does other work |
| Best for | Very fast, predictable devices | Slow, unpredictable devices |
| Overhead per event | None extra | Context save/restore |

Too many interrupts (a flood of tiny ones) can flip the trade-off back toward polling.

blocks.subTitle: The request
blocks.markdown:
An **interrupt request (IRQ)** is a signal a device sends on the control bus to say "I need attention now."

- The CPU finishes its current instruction, then checks for pending IRQs before fetching the next one.
- Each device line maps to a number, so the CPU knows *which* device is asking.

blocks.subTitle: Context save and the handler
blocks.markdown:
Handling an interrupt has three steps:

- **Context save** — push the current program counter and registers, so the interrupted program can resume exactly where it left off.
- **Run the ISR (interrupt service handler)** — a small routine that services the device (e.g., reads a keystroke).
- **Context restore** — pop the saved state back and resume the original program.

The CPU can't scan every possible handler on each interrupt — that's too slow. Instead, an **interrupt vector table** maps each interrupt number directly to the memory address of its ISR.

- On an IRQ, the CPU looks up the number, jumps straight to that address.
- Fixed, indexed lookup — O(1) dispatch instead of a search.

The full round trip from device to resumed program.

Every interrupt-driven device follows this same loop, only the ISR's job changes.

Common mistakes:

- **"DMA removes the CPU from I/O entirely."** No — the CPU still sets up the transfer and handles the completion interrupt.
- **"Interrupts are always faster than polling."** Not for very fast devices — the context-save overhead can cost more than a quick check would.
- **"Memory-mapped I/O is slower."** It isn't inherently slower; it just shares the address space instead of using separate instructions.

blocks.subTitle: Polling vs interrupts
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Polling vs interrupts — when would you choose each?**

**Polling** when the device is fast and its response time is predictable — the check is cheaper than an interrupt's context-switch overhead. **Interrupts** when the device is slow or unpredictable, so the CPU can do useful work while waiting instead of spinning.

blocks.subTitle: What DMA solves
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is DMA and why does it help?**

DMA is a controller that transfers data between a device and memory directly, without routing every byte through the CPU. It helps because the CPU only sets up the transfer and handles one completion interrupt — freeing it to run other instructions during a large disk or network transfer.

blocks.subTitle: How an interrupt works
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Walk through what happens when an interrupt fires.**

The device raises an IRQ on the control bus. The CPU finishes its current instruction, saves its context (program counter, registers), looks up the interrupt vector table to find the right ISR, runs it, then restores context and resumes exactly where it left off.

blocks.subTitle: Memory-mapped vs port-mapped
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Memory-mapped vs port-mapped I/O — what's the real difference?**

Memory-mapped I/O puts device registers in the normal address space, so ordinary load/store instructions reach them. Port-mapped I/O keeps a separate address space reachable only through special IN/OUT instructions. Most modern systems use memory-mapped I/O since it needs no dedicated instruction set.
